# Titthajātaka (Ja 25)

**ID:** Ja 25
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Titthajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

According to the traditional account in the Jātaka commentary, the Buddha related this story while residing at Jetavana regarding an ex-goldsmith who had ordained as a monk and become a co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*) of Sāriputta, the "Captain of the Faith" (*dhammasenāpati*) [Fausböll 1877]. The commentary introduces the tale to demonstrate that only a Buddha possesses full insight into the underlying intentions and latent dispositions (*āsayānusayañāṇa*) of others [Fausböll 1877; Heim 2014].

In the narrative of the past, accompanied by the verse incipit *Aññamaññehi titthehi* ("Change thou the spot"), the Bodhisatta appears as a wise court minister (*paṇḍita-amacca*) [Fausböll 1877]. Observing a pampered royal state horse (*maṅgalassa*) that refuses to enter the water, the Bodhisatta deduces the animal's thoughts and bruised feelings upon finding that other, ordinary horses had sullied the bathing-place, advising that it be led to an alternate spot [Fausböll 1877; Heim 2014]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the state horse as the goldsmith monk, the king as Ānanda, and the discerning minister as the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1877].
